web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Ten-Year Financial Forensics — Margin Compression, Cash Conversion & Capital Allocation
question: What does a ten-year forensic audit of Nike's P&L, cash conversion, ROIC, and balance sheet reveal about the durability of its economic engine?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion shaped by accruals and one-time recoveries; operating cash flow minus capital expenditures is the only check you can actually cash.
epigraph.author: Chapter 6 Financial Forensics

web_blocks.html: From FY2017 through FY2026, NIKE, Inc. grew consolidated revenue from $34,350 million to $46,398 million [1, 20]. That 3.4% ten-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR) hides two sharply different halves. Between FY2017 and FY2024, revenue rose $17.0 billion (+49.5%) to a $51,362 million peak on pandemic stimulus, digital adoption, and Greater China growth [10, 20]. Since FY2024, revenue has dropped $5.0 billion (-9.7%) and stayed weak in Q1 FY2027 ($11.2 billion, -4% YoY) [1, 3]. That reversal turned a steady multi-year compounder into an operational turnaround.

Margin compression has been far steeper than the top-line decline. Gross margin held in a tight 43.4%–46.0% band from FY2017 to FY2024 [20]. It then fell 190 bps to 42.7% in FY2025 before edging up 20 bps to 42.9% in FY2026 [1, 20]. Operating income peaked at $6,937 million in FY2021 (15.6% margin) and $6,311 million in FY2024 (12.3%) [20]. It dropped 41% in FY2025 to $3,702 million (8.0%) and nudged up to $3,797 million in FY2026 (8.2%) [1, 20]. Even FY2026's $3,850 million reported EBIT ($3,108 million net income) leaned on $986 million in one-time IEEPA tariff recoveries booked in Q4 FY2026 [1, 2].

web_blocks.title: 6.2 Cash Conversion, ROIC & Balance Sheet Forensics

web_blocks.html: Historically, Nike converted 100% to 130% of Net Income into Operating Cash Flow (CFO) [20]. That ratio peaked at $7,429 million CFO and $6,617 million Free Cash Flow (FCF) in FY2024 (130% CFO/NI conversion) [20]. In FY2026, CFO fell to $2,868 million (92% of Net Income), and FCF dropped to $2,184 million—below the $2,407 million dividend [1, 20]. That squeeze forced Nike to virtually halt share buybacks ($146 million in FY2026 vs. $4,250 million in FY2024 and $5,480 million in FY2023) [1, 20]. Even with compressed earnings, Nike's asset-light model posts a trailing Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) near 13.0% (12.99%). That still clears an estimated 8%–9% cost of capital, though it trails Nike's historical 25%–30%+ ROIC peaks.

On the balance sheet, raw cash liquidity remains sizable, but footnote and lease forensics reveal far less cushion than headline net cash implies. On May 31, 2026, Nike held $7,563 million in cash and equivalents plus $1,464 million in short-term investments ($9,027 million total) against $7,942 million of funded debt ($5,942 million long-term debt plus $2,000 million current portion) [1]. However, including $3,091 million of balance-sheet operating lease liabilities ($478 million current + $2,613 million non-current), total debt was $11,033 million—putting Nike in a ~$2,006 million lease-adjusted net debt position. By Q1 FY2027 (August 31, 2026, Form 10-Q), that squeeze tightened: despite collecting substantially all of the remaining $684 million IEEPA tariff receivable (+$695 million AR inflow), Q1 operating cash flow fell to just $135 million (vs. $222 million prior year) due to -$1,219 million in payables/accrued liability outflows (including $243 million in severance payments) and +$312 million in inventory additions ($7,846 million total). After $199 million of CapEx and $610 million in dividends, cash & short-term investments fell $659 million in one quarter to $8,368 million against $7,893 million funded debt and $3,179 million operating lease liabilities ($473M current + $2,706M non-current), widening lease-adjusted net debt to $2,704 million.

Off-Balance-Sheet Commitments, Credit Downgrades & Capital-Return Math: FY2026 Form 10-K disclosures reveal ~$22.8 billion in contractual purchase and endorsement commitments that act like quasi-fixed operating leverage during a revenue downturn. As of May 31, 2026, Nike carried ~$15.5 billion in endorsement contract obligations (~$1.7 billion payable within 12 months, before product-furnishing costs and performance bonuses), ~$4.9 billion in product purchase obligations (~$4.7 billion within 12 months), and ~$2.4 billion in other purchase obligations (~$1.6 billion within 12 months). Because athlete and league guarantees cannot be cut quickly, they amplify operating deleverage—helping explain why both S&P Global Ratings and Moody's Ratings downgraded NIKE's credit ratings in 2025 (while remaining Investment Grade ahead of $2,000 million in current debt maturities) and why FY2027 adjusted operating margin is guided to ~6%. Add ~$1.3 billion in cumulative Pace pre-tax restructuring charges ($0.3B FY26, $0.3B FY27, mainly cash severance), $1.1 billion in supplier finance payables, and an unestimable Belgian Customs duty contingency (Q1 10-Q Note 11). With Nov 17 Investor Day guidance at $1.15–$1.35 FY2027 adjusted EPS alongside ~$2.4 billion annual dividends (~$12 billion cumulative FY27–FY31), dividends will exceed near-term earnings and free cash flow—keeping share buybacks essentially frozen and drawing down cash reserves until margins recover.

web_blocks.title: The Capital-Allocation Inflection
paragraphs: For a decade, Nike funded rising dividends ($1.13B to $2.41B) and large buybacks ($3B–$5.5B/year) from internal FCF [20]. In FY2026, FCF of $2,184M fell $223M short of the $2,407M dividend [1, 20], and Q1 FY2027 produced -$64M FCF ($135M CFO less $199M CapEx) even after collecting the IEEPA tariff receivable. With FY2027 adjusted EPS guided to $1.15–$1.35 (~$1.7B–$2.0B earnings) against ~$2.4B in committed annual dividends (~$12B FY27–FY31) and ~$1.3B in Pace restructuring charges, share buybacks remain effectively suspended while Nike draws on liquidity.

book_paragraphs: When you put Nike's ten-year financial statements under a forensic microscope, the story splits cleanly into two acts. In Act One, from FY2017 through FY2024, Nike looked like an unstoppable compounding machine: revenue climbed from $34.35 billion to $51.36 billion, gross margins hovered between 43.4% and 46.0%, and free cash flow hit $6.62 billion in FY2024. That river of cash let Nike double its annual dividend from $1.13 billion to $2.17 billion while retiring $3 billion to $5.5 billion of shares almost every single year.

In Act Two—FY2025 and FY2026—that engine hit a wall. Revenue stepped down 10% to $46.31 billion in FY2025 and flatlined at $46.40 billion in FY2026. Operating income compressed from $6.31 billion in FY2024 to $3.80 billion in FY2026, slicing operating margin from 12.3% down to 8.2%. And remember our Chapter 2 footnote: even FY2026's profit benefited from $986 million in one-time IEEPA tariff recoveries booked in Q4. Without that windfall, underlying operating earnings were noticeably thinner.

Now follow the cash, because cash never lies. In FY2026, operating cash flow fell to $2.87 billion, and after $684 million of capital expenditures, Free Cash Flow landed at $2.18 billion—roughly one-third of FY2024's $6.62 billion. In Q1 FY2027 (ended August 31, 2026), even after collecting substantially all of the remaining $684 million IEEPA tariff refund receivable, operating cash flow slumped to just $135 million as accrued liabilities and payables dropped $1.22 billion and inventories swelled by $312 million to $7.85 billion—producing negative $64 million of Free Cash Flow. Meanwhile, Nike's board committed at the November 17, 2026 Investor Day to roughly $2.4 billion per year ($12 billion cumulative through FY2031) in dividends while guiding FY2027 adjusted EPS to just $1.15 to $1.35 and earmarking $1.3 billion in Pace severance/restructuring charges. When dividends exceed earnings and free cash flow, buybacks stay frozen and cash reserves shrink—down $659 million in Q1 alone.

What keeps this operational squeeze from becoming a solvency crisis is Nike's $8.37 billion cash and short-term investment buffer at August 31, 2026—yet footnote forensics show the balance sheet is tighter than headline numbers suggest. Add $3.18 billion of balance-sheet operating lease liabilities to $7.89 billion of funded debt, and Nike actually sits in roughly $2.70 billion of lease-adjusted net debt rather than net cash. Even more important, the FY2026 10-K discloses $15.5 billion in off-balance-sheet endorsement contract obligations ($1.7 billion due within 12 months) alongside $7.3 billion in product and other purchase obligations—a rigid fixed-cost floor that already contributed to 2025 credit-rating downgrades by both S&P Global Ratings and Moody's Ratings. Combined with $1.1 billion in supplier finance payables and an unestimable Belgian Customs duty appeal, Nike remains Investment Grade with ample runway to execute 'Pace,' but its margin for error is far narrower than during its 25%+ ROIC compounding era.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When a serial share-repurchaser slashes buybacks by 95% to protect its dividend, the cash-flow statement is telling you far more about operational stress than any management slide deck.

book_subsections.title: Working Capital, Debt Maturity & Dividend Coverage Forensics
paragraphs: Let us look even closer at why Operating Cash Flow dropped to $2,868 million in FY2026 despite $3,108 million of reported Net Income. Remember that Q4 FY2026 Net Income benefited from $986 million in expected IEEPA tariff recovery bookings—non-cash or timing-lagged receivables that boosted accounting profit faster than cash hit the bank. At the same time, carrying $7,501 million of inventory while resetting wholesale terms tied up working capital, leaving Free Cash Flow at $2,184 million—$223 million short of the $2,407 million dividend.

On the liability and commitment side, Nike's balance sheet carries meaningful fixed obligations that investors often overlook. Alongside $7,893 million in funded debt ($2,000 million current) at August 31, 2026, Nike holds $3,179 million in operating lease liabilities—turning headline net cash into $2,704 million of lease-adjusted net debt—plus $1.1 billion in voluntary supplier finance payables and an unresolved Belgian Customs duty appeal backed by bank guarantees. Off the balance sheet, the FY2026 10-K discloses $15.5 billion in endorsement guarantees (~$1.7 billion due within 12 months) and $7.3 billion in product and other purchase commitments. Following 2025 rating downgrades by S&P and Moody's (while keeping Investment Grade status) and ~$1.3 billion in planned Pace restructuring charges, Nike's capital allocation has shifted squarely from buyback compounding to defensive dividend funding (~$2.4B/year) while waiting for margins to trough in FY2027.

book_subsections.title: Two Acts on the Ten-Year P&L: From 15.6% Peak to the Tariff Cushion
paragraphs: Spread Nike's ten-year income statements across your desk from FY2017 through FY2026, and you see a 3.4% ten-year revenue compound annual growth rate—from $34,350 million to $46,398 million—that disguises two completely different eras. In Act One, spanning FY2017 through FY2024, revenue expanded by $17.0 billion, or 49.5%, to a peak of $51,362 million, propelled by pandemic stimulus, digital adoption, and Greater China expansion. Gross margins held reliably between 43.4% and 46.0%, while operating income peaked at $6,937 million in FY2021 (a 15.6% margin) and $6,311 million in FY2024 (12.3%). Aside from FY2018's one-time U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act transition charges that temporarily depressed Net Income to $1,933 million, Nike looked like an effortless earnings machine.

Act Two—FY2025 and FY2026—broke that rhythm. Revenue contracted by $5.0 billion, or 9.7%, from its FY2024 peak and stayed soft in Q1 FY2027 at $11.2 billion (-4% YoY). Gross margin dropped 190 basis points to 42.7% in FY2025 and recovered just 20 basis points to 42.9% in FY2026, while operating income fell 41% in FY2025 to $3,702 million (8.0% margin) and edged up only modestly to $3,797 million (8.2%) in FY2026. Remember the forensic footnote we uncovered earlier: even FY2026's $3,850 million reported EBIT and $3,108 million Net Income leaned on $986 million in one-time IEEPA tariff recovery benefits recognized in Q4, meaning underlying operating profitability was noticeably thinner.

book_subsections.title: Cash Conversion, ROIC Compression, and the Buyback Freeze
paragraphs: Now follow the cash-flow statement, because accrual accounting can flatter a turnaround quarter while cash conversion tells you the unvarnished truth. Historically, Nike converted 100% to 130% of Net Income into Operating Cash Flow, peaking at $7,429 million CFO and $6,617 million Free Cash Flow in FY2024—a 130% CFO-to-Net-Income conversion ratio. In FY2026, CFO dropped to $2,868 million (92% of Net Income) and Free Cash Flow fell to $2,184 million, a 4.7% FCF margin that sat roughly one-third of FY2024's level. Because Nike's dividend commitment had grown steadily from $1,130 million in FY2017 to $2,407 million in FY2026, Free Cash Flow fell $223 million short of covering the dividend. That explains why share repurchases—which ran between $2,990 million and $5,480 million a year from FY2022 through FY2025—were slashed 95% to just $146 million in FY2026.

What keeps this operational squeeze from becoming a solvency problem is Nike's fortress balance sheet. At May 31, 2026, Nike held $38,410 million in total assets and $14,865 million in shareholders' equity, with a 2.07x current ratio and $9,027 million in cash and short-term investments against $7,942 million in total funded debt—a net cash position of $1,085 million generating $50 million of net interest income. Even with trailing ROIC compressed to roughly 13.0% (12.99%) from historical 25%–30%+ peaks, Nike still clears an estimated 8%–9% cost of capital and holds plenty of liquidity to fund 'Pace' while defending its dividend.
